title: Stage 5: Production hardening
summary: Pinned, chiseled, non-root, limited and checked: turn the working image into one you can run in production.

steps.title: The hardened version
body: - **pinned** SDK patch version and a lock file with `--locked-mode`: the same commit builds the same image;
- **chiseled** runtime: no shell, no package manager, far fewer CVEs; non-root by default, and `USER $APP_UID` makes it explicit;
- **read-only** root filesystem, **memory and CPU limits**, a **restart policy**, **rotated logs**;
- the image is deployed by an immutable version tag built in CI, never `latest`.

steps.prompt: With the chiseled image, a Docker `HEALTHCHECK` using `curl` no longer works. What is a sound approach?
options: Let the orchestrator probe `/health` over HTTP from outside (Kubernetes probes), or ship a tiny health-probe binary in the image
Install curl with apt-get in the final stage
Switch back to the SDK image
steps.explain: Chiseled images have no package manager by design. Kubernetes HTTP probes need nothing inside the container.

items: Log rotation with max-size and max-file
A chiseled base with no shell
A memory limit and restart policy

steps.prompt: With `read_only: true`, the app crashes writing to `/tmp`. What is the right fix?
options: Mount a tmpfs at /tmp (`tmpfs: [/tmp]` in Compose) so only that path is writable, in memory

steps.title: Harden it and run it locked down
prompt: This terminal has a **real Docker Engine** with the .NET images and the working multi-stage `~/todo/Dockerfile`
(built as `todo:2`). Make it production-ready and build it as `todo:3`:
2. the final stage runs as the **non-root** user the .NET images provide (`$APP_UID`);
3. the image has a `HEALTHCHECK` on `/health` (the Alpine-based image has `wget`).
Then run it as a container named `todo` on port 8080 with a **read-only** root filesystem (with a tmpfs for
`/tmp`), **all capabilities dropped** and **no-new-privileges**, and wait until it is `healthy`.

checks.name: docker build --check is clean
checks.fail: `docker build --check` still warns (or the Dockerfile does not build).

checks.name: todo:3 runs as a non-root user with a healthcheck
checks.cmd: docker image inspect -f '{{.Config.User}}' todo:3; docker run --rm --entrypoint id todo:3 -u; docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Healthcheck.Test}}' todo:3 | grep -c /health
checks.fail: `todo:3` should run as `$APP_UID` (not root) and have a `HEALTHCHECK` that requests `/health`.

checks.name: todo runs locked down
checks.cmd: docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Image}} ro={{.HostConfig.ReadonlyRootfs}} caps={{.HostConfig.CapDrop}} sec={{.HostConfig.SecurityOpt}} tmpfs={{.HostConfig.Tmpfs}}' todo

checks.name: it is healthy and serves /health
checks.fail: `todo` is not healthy yet (or does not answer on 8080).

hints: The .NET images define a non-root user and its ID in `$APP_UID`: `USER $APP_UID` in the final stage.
solution: sed -i 's#^ENTRYPOINT \["dotnet", "TodoApi.dll"\]#USER $APP_UID\nHEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1\nENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "TodoApi.dll"]#' Dockerfile
docker run -d --name todo -p 8080:8080 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges:true todo:3
steps.explain: Each layer of defence takes one line: a non-root user (the official .NET images ship one, `app`, UID 1654), a read-only root filesystem so an attacker cannot drop tools into the container, no Linux capabilities and no privilege escalation. A .NET API runs happily under all of them, and the healthcheck lets Docker, Compose or your orchestrator see the difference between "running" and "answering". Kubernetes expresses the same settings in `securityContext`.
